{{Short description|Disproved conjecture in ring theory}}
In [[mathematics]], the '''Köthe conjecture''' is a problem in [[ring theory]]. It is formulated in various ways. Suppose that ''R'' is a [[ring (mathematics)|ring]]. One way to state the [[conjecture]] is that if ''R'' has no [[nil ideal]], other than {0}, then it has no nil [[one-sided ideal]], other than {0}.

This question was posed in 1930 by [[Gottfried Köthe]] (1905–1989). The Köthe conjecture has been shown to be true for various classes of rings, such as [[polynomial identity ring]]s<ref>{{cite book |first1=John C. |last1=McConnell |first2=James Christopher |last2=Robson |first3=Lance W. |last3=Small |title=Noncommutative Noetherian rings |year=2001 |page=484 |isbn=9780821821695 |series=Graduate Studies in Mathematics |volume=30 |publisher=American Mathematical Society |url=https://archive.org/details/noncommutativeno0000mcco? |url-access=registration |via=archive.org}}</ref> and right [[Noetherian ring]]s.<ref>{{cite book |author-link=Tsit Yuen Lam |last=Lam |first=T. Y. |title=A First Course in Noncommutative Rings |year=2001 |page=164 |doi=10.1007/978-1-4419-8616-0 |isbn=978-0-387-95183-6 |url=https://archive.org/details/firstcourseinnon0000lamt |url-access=registration |via=archive.org}}
</ref> In 2026, the AI model [[GPT-6 Astra]] found an explicit counterexample which disproves the conjecture, after being prompted by Tom Adamczewski of Epoch AI.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Köthe conjecture: disproof (Krempa's matrix form) |url=https://github.com/tadamcz/koethe |website=Github}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |title=Köthe Conjecture |url=https://vibemathed.com/problem/kothe-conjecture |website=VibeMathed |access-date=7 September 2026 |language=en |date=4 September 2026}}</ref> An exposition of the proof was posted by Adamczewski and ring theorists Bernhard Böhmler and Rene Marczinzik.<ref>{{cite arXiv |last1=Adamczewski |first1=Tom |title=A counterexample to Köthe's conjecture and a question of Rowen |date=2026-09-07 |eprint=2609.07996 |last2=Böhmler |first2=Bernhard |last3=Marczinzik |first3=Rene |class=math.RA }}</ref> Another counterexample was found by Greenfeld, King and Vendramin, with some assistance from GPT-6 Astra.<ref>{{Cite arXiv|last1=Greenfeld |first1=B. |last2=King |first2=B. |last3=Vendramin |first3=L. |title=The Köthe conjecture via point modules |date=2026 |language=en |arxiv=2609.15080 |class=math.RA }}</ref>

==Equivalent formulations==
The conjecture has several different formulations:<ref>{{cite journal |last=Krempa |first=Jan |title=Logical connections between some open problems concerning nil rings |journal=Fundamenta Mathematicae |series=76 |year=1972 |volume=76 |issue=2 |page=121&ndash;130 |doi=10.4064/fm-76-2-121-130 |doi-access=free |s2cid=119012657}}</ref><ref>Lam, T. Y., ''A First Course in Noncommutative Rings'' (2001), p. 171.</ref><ref>{{cite book |first=T. Y. |last=Lam |title=Exercises in Classical Ring Theory |year=2003 |page=160 |isbn=9780387005003 |doi=10.1007/b97448|publisher=Springer}}</ref>
# (Köthe conjecture) In any ring, the [[Ideal (ring theory)#Ideal operations|sum]] of two nil left ideals is nil.
# In any ring, the sum of two one-sided nil ideals is nil. 
# In any ring, every nil left or right ideal of the ring is contained in the [[Radical of a ring#The upper nil radical or K.C3.B6the radical|upper nil radical]] of the ring.
# For any ring ''R'' and for any nil ideal ''J'' of ''R'', the [[matrix (mathematics)|matrix]] ideal M<sub>''n''</sub>(''J'') is a nil ideal of M<sub>''n''</sub>(''R'') for every ''n''.
# For any ring ''R'' and for any nil ideal ''J'' of ''R'', the matrix ideal M<sub>2</sub>(''J'') is a nil ideal of M<sub>2</sub>(''R'').
# For any ring ''R'', the upper nil radical of M<sub>''n''</sub>(''R'') is the set of matrices with entries from the upper nilradical of ''R'' for every positive integer ''n''.
# For any ring ''R'' and for any nil ideal ''J'' of ''R'', the [[polynomial]]s with indeterminate ''x'' and [[coefficient]]s from ''J'' lie in the [[Jacobson radical]] of the [[polynomial ring]] ''R''[''x''].
# For any ring ''R'', the Jacobson radical of ''R''[''x''] consists of the polynomials with coefficients from the upper nilradical of ''R''.

Necessary and sufficient conditions under which statement 3 given above does not hold have been given recently.<ref>{{cite journal |last=Pandey |first=S. K. |title=A note on upper nilradicals and one-sided nil ideals |journal=Serdica Mathematical Journal |series=50 |year=2024 |volume=3-4 |doi=10.55630/serdica.2024.50.3 |doi-broken-date=20 September 2026 |doi-access=free}}</ref>

==Related problems==
A conjecture by [[Shimshon Amitsur|Amitsur]] read: "If ''J'' is a nil ideal in ''R'', then ''J''[''x''] is a nil ideal of the polynomial ring ''R''[''x'']."<ref>{{cite book |last=Amitsur |first=S. A. |chapter=Nil radicals. Historical notes and some new results |title=Rings, modules and radicals (Proc. Internat. Colloq., Keszthely, 1971) |pages=47–65 |series=Colloq. Math. Soc. János Bolyai |volume=6 |publisher=North-Holland |year=1973 |isbn=0720420709 |via=archive.org |url-access=registration |url=https://archive.org/details/ringsmodulesradi0000unse_l6j7}}</ref> This conjecture, if true, would have [[mathematical proof|proven]] the Köthe conjecture through the equivalent statements above. However, in 2000 a [[counterexample]] was produced by [[Agata Smoktunowicz]].<ref>[[Agata Smoktunowicz|Smoktunowicz, Agata]]. ''Polynomial rings over nil rings need not be nil'' J. Algebra 233 (2000), no. 2, p. 427–436.</ref> While not a disproof of the Köthe conjecture, this fueled suspicions that the Köthe conjecture may be false.<ref>Lam, T.Y., ''A First Course in Noncommutative Rings'' (2001), p.171.</ref>

[[Otto H. Kegel|Kegel]] proved a ring which is the direct sum of two nilpotent [[subring]]s is itself [[nilpotent]].<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Kegel |first=Otto H. |date=1964-07-01 |title=On rings that are sums of two subrings |journal=Journal of Algebra |volume=1 |issue=2 |pages=103–109 |doi=10.1016/0021-8693(64)90026-2 |doi-access=free}}</ref> The question arose whether or not "nilpotent" could be replaced with "locally nilpotent" or "nil". Partial progress was made when Kelarev produced an example of a ring which isn't nil, but is the direct sum of two locally nilpotent rings. This demonstrates that Kegel's question with "locally nilpotent" replacing "nilpotent" is answered in the negative.<ref>Kelarev, A. V., A sum of two locally nilpotent rings may not be nil, Arch. Math. 60 (1993), p431–435.</ref>

The sum of a nilpotent subring and a nil subring is always nil.<ref>Ferrero, M., Puczylowski, E. R., On rings which are sums of two subrings, Arch. Math. 53 (1989), p4–10.</ref>
